Friends from school (in south London) Sheppard and Phelan began experimental recordings in 1996, soon hooking up with percussionist Steele to leaven their intertwining, Nick Drake-like acoustic guitars with vigorous yet dexterous drumming.

The band's debut single, "Unsung Couples", was released on the Gold Hole label in November 1998. SRW’s hypnotic cycles of avant-rock melody connected with an audience then thrilling to similarly inclined practitioners such as Godspeed You! Black Emperor and Tortoise.

Further singles and compilation tracks appeared before the November 1999 release of SRW’s eponymous debut (on rising independent imprint Rocket Girl), drawing plaudits from Delusions of Adequacy, who observed that the band's "intoxicating back-to-nature acoustic explorations supplied the Anglo-agrarian answer to Chicago's urbanite post-rock crowd". Released in spring 2003, the album proved another critical success, with several Early Music tracks finding their way onto TV documentary and advertising soundtracks.

Recorded between late 2003 and spring 2004, the album Cottonhead was released at the end of October 2004 on a new label, Vertical Form. In 2005, Phelan and Sheppard signed (under their own names) to The Leaf Label and at the end of the year began work on a new album, with ex-Laika mainstay Guy Fixsen assisting. That album, Harps Old Master, was released in September 2006.

prompt: What is the difference between a fetus and an infant, and when does the fetus become an infant?
response_a:
A fetus refers to an unborn baby who is developing inside its mother's womb from conception until birth. During this stage, which lasts approximately 9 months, the fetus undergoes rapid physical and developmental changes. The fetus is completely dependent on the mother's body for nourishment, oxygen, and protection.

An infant, on the other hand, is a newborn baby who has been born and is now outside of their mother's womb. This stage begins at birth and continues until the child reaches the age of 1 year. Infants require constant care and attention as they are not yet able to regulate their own bodily functions such as breathing, feeding, and eliminating waste.

In summary, the main difference between a fetus and an infant is that a fetus is still developing inside the mother's womb, while an infant has already been born and is now outside the womb. The transition from fetus to infant occurs at birth.
response_b:
A fetus refers to an unborn baby who is developing inside its mother's womb. The term "fetus" is typically used during the later stages of pregnancy, from around week 9 or 10 until birth. During this time, the fetus continues to grow and develop essential organs and body systems.

An infant, on the other hand, refers to a newborn baby who has been born and is now outside the mother's womb. This stage begins at birth and continues through the first year of life. During infancy, the baby will continue to develop physically, mentally, and emotionally as they learn to adapt to life outside the womb.

In summary, the main difference between a fetus and an infant is that a fetus is an unborn baby still developing in the womb, while an infant is a newborn baby who has already been born. The transition from fetus to infant occurs at birth.

Long charging times and a lack of public chargers are keeping people from buying electric cars. 
Some startups are convinced that EV charging needs a fundamental overhaul. 
Battery swapping and wireless EV charging could someday make owning an EV way more convenient. 
The thought of charging is scaring away potential electric car buyers. If everybody is expected to shun dirty fuels sooner rather than later, that needs to change.  
Sure, automakers can tackle the frustratingly long duration of charging stops by engineering cars that recharge more quickly and drive farther between fill-ups. Charging providers can put anxious drivers at ease by blanketing the country with a greater number of more reliable stations. And that's all happening. 
But some startups are convinced the way we refuel EVs needs a complete overhaul. 
When a battery dies, swap it
San Francisco-based Ample's pitch is simple: Instead of spending precious time waiting around to refill the same battery over and over, why not simply change it out for a fresh pack and be on your way? 
Ample's drive-through battery-swapping stations, roughly the size of a few parking spaces, are where the magic happens. After a driver pulls into a stall, their vehicle is lifted up and machinery below springs into action, autonomously plucking out the depleted pack and replacing it with a fully charged one in minutes. That's a game-changing improvement over typical fast-charging stations, where getting a solid charge could take 30 minutes to an hour or more. 
The firm is still in its very early days, but its tech is already in the hands of some Uber drivers in California thanks to a deal with the ride-hailing giant. Ample plans to focus on taxi, delivery, and car-rental fleets before turning its attention to regular consumers. 
You won't be able to pull up to an Ample station in just any EV — it'll need to be outfitted with the startup's modular, removable battery packs. The company plans to accomplish that through partnerships with automakers. 
Given our currently limited infrastructure and technology, EVs work best for people who don't drive very far in a day and can charge at home. Quick, convenient, and cheap battery swapping will be key for getting everyone else on board, John de Souza, Ample's cofounder and president, told Insider. 
"If you don't have the luxury of having a parking garage overnight, it starts falling apart," he said, referring to EV ownership. "Or if you drive a lot of miles, it falls apart."
Ample offers more than just speedy pit stops, de Souza said. Under the company's model, customers will buy a battery-less vehicle and then pay a battery subscription, potentially slashing the upfront cost of going electric. Battery swapping should extend vehicle longevity by cutting down on fast-charging sessions, which accelerate battery wear, and by letting owners keep up with the latest advances in battery chemistry, de Souza said. 
Chinese startup Nio has sold cars with swappable batteries for years while building out the infrastructure to support them — first in its homeland and now in Europe. Stateside, widespread battery swapping still looks a long way off, but it's gaining momentum. US EV startup Fisker recently announced plans to offer Ample's tech in its Ocean SUV starting in 2024. 
Electric cars, meet electric roads
For Israel's Electreon, the path toward an EV future is paved with roads that wirelessly recharge vehicles while they're moving.
The tech may sound like something straight out of science fiction, but it's real. Electreon's initial projects mainly bring wireless charging to public buses — vehicles with predictable routes and depots ripe for reinvention. But it's not stopping there. 
Oren Ezer, Electreon's cofounder and CEO, told Insider that wireless charging could solve the biggest challenges stunting the EV revolution: insufficient charging infrastructure, limited driving range, and a reliance on large, expensive batteries. In a world where electrified bus stops, parking spots, and streets charge vehicles all the time, those sticking points recede into the rearview. That's the long-term vision, anyway. 
To demonstrate the transformative potential of so-called "dynamic wireless charging," Electreon in May set out to drive a Toyota RAV4 Prime — a plug-in hybrid with just 42 miles of electric-only range — for 100 hours straight without plugging in or using any gas. 
On a test track with its copper charging coils embedded in the asphalt, Electreon and a team of 55 drivers covered 1,207 miles, a feat that would be unthinkable in a typical EV. (The cream of today's electric crop can travel 300-500 miles before they need to stop and recharge.)
The SUV, specially outfitted to receive energy wirelessly, looped the track at around 20-30 mph, Ezer said. He added that even at highway speeds, Electreon's roads can keep a vehicle's battery topped up indefinitely. 
Before you shudder at the prospect of endless, invasive construction if this tech takes off, consider this: Electreon says it can lay 1 mile of road in a night. It doesn't need to rip up an entire street, Ezer said, just dig a trench about three inches deep. 
Despite the billions pouring into conventional charging infrastructure, Ezer thinks his technology will win out someday. One positive sign: In March, Electreon announced an R&D partnership with Toyota. 
"We need all the solutions together in order to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles," he said. "But wireless will be dominant for sure."

prompt: What are some ways to build self-confidence, especially during a job interview?
response_a:
1. Preparation: One of the most effective ways to build self-confidence during a job interview is to be well-prepared. Research the company and its values, practice answering common interview questions, and prepare examples of your past work experiences that demonstrate your skills and abilities.

2. Positive Self-Talk: It's essential to have positive self-talk before and during the interview. Instead of focusing on negative thoughts or doubts, replace them with positive affirmations about your qualifications, experience, and potential for success in the role.

3. Practice Deep Breathing and Relaxation Techniques: Nerves can cause physical symptoms like sweating, shaking, and rapid breathing. To manage these symptoms, practice deep breathing exercises and relaxation techniques like meditation or progressive muscle relaxation to help you stay calm and focused during the interview.

4. Dress Appropriately: Wearing clothing that makes you feel confident and comfortable will help boost your self-esteem during the interview. Choose an outfit that fits well, flatters your body type, and makes you feel confident and professional.

5. Make Eye Contact: Making eye contact with the interviewer shows confidence and helps establish a connection. Remember to maintain good posture and avoid fidgeting or playing with your hands as this can make you appear nervous or unsure.

6. Listen Carefully: During the interview, listen carefully to the interviewer's questions and respond thoughtfully. This demonstrates that you understand the requirements of the position and are a good fit for the company culture.

7. Ask Questions: Asking insightful questions about the company, the role, and the team demonstrates your interest in the opportunity and your commitment to learning more about the organization. This also provides an opportunity to clarify any concerns you may have about the position.

8. Follow Up: After the interview, follow up with a thank-you note or email to the interviewer, reiterating your enthusiasm for the position and expressing gratitude for the opportunity to learn more about the company. This shows that you value the time and effort the interviewer has put into the process and reinforces your interest in the position.

Remember, building self-confidence takes practice, so continue to work on developing these habits both before and during future interviews. With persistence and dedication, you'll gradually improve your confidence level, making it easier to ace your next job interview!
response_b:

2. Positive self-talk: Before and during the interview, focus on positive self-talk. Remind yourself of your strengths, accomplishments, and reasons why you're a great fit for the position. Avoid negative self-talk or comparisons with others.

3. Body language: Nonverbal communication can have a significant impact on how others perceive us. Maintain good posture, make eye contact, and smile. These gestures can project confidence and engagement.

4. Active listening: Show that you're an active listener by asking clarifying questions and summarizing what the interviewer has said. This not only demonstrates your interest in the company but also helps you better understand the job requirements.

5. Positivity: Stay positive throughout the interview. Even if you're asked challenging questions, remain optimistic and solutions-focused. Focus on how you can contribute to the company rather than dwelling on past mistakes or failures.

6. Breathing exercises: Take deep breaths before the interview to calm your nerves. This can help you feel more centered and focused, which can translate into increased confidence.

7. Visualization: Picture yourself succeeding in the interview. Imagine yourself answering questions confidently and impressing the interviewer. This visualization can help you approach the interview with a positive mindset.

8. Seek feedback: After the interview, ask for feedback from the interviewer or recruiter. This can help you identify areas where you need improvement and give you insight into how you came across during the interview. Use this feedback constructively to build your confidence for future interviews.

Remember, building self-confidence takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself and celebrate small wins along the way. With consistent effort, you'll gradually build the confidence you need to excel in job interviews and beyond!

Although Brutus justified his actions as being for the good of Rome, many considered him an ingrate for turning on a man who had shown him so much kindness and trust.

2. Benedict Arnold: During the American Revolutionary War, Benedict Arnold was a highly decorated general in the Continental Army. However, he switched sides and became a traitor to the cause when he sold West Point to the British in 1780. Arnold's betrayal was a major blow to the American effort, and he is often remembered as one of the most infamous ingrates in history.

3. Judas Iscariot: In Christianity, Judas is best known as the disciple who betrayed Jesus Christ to the authorities. He received money from the chief priests as payment for identifying Jesus at the Last Supper, and then went on to hang himself after realizing the extent of his wrongdoing. Judas' betrayal is considered one of the greatest acts of ingratitude in religious history.

4. Richard III: The last Plantagenet king of England, Richard III, has long been portrayed as a villainous figure due to his role in the deaths of several members of the House of York. His actions included orchestrating the murder of his nephews, the Princes in the Tower, which has earned him the reputation of an ingrate and a tyrant.

5. Lucretia Borgia: As the daughter of the powerful Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, Lucretia Borgia enjoyed a privileged position in Renaissance Italy. However, she is infamous for using her beauty and charm to manipulate men into doing her bidding, including arranging the murders of several husbands and lovers. Her actions have led many to view her as an ingrate who abused the opportunities given to her by her family.

6. King George III: In the lead-up to the American Revolution, King George III played a significant role in the decisions that led to conflict between Britain and its colonies. Many Americans saw him as an ingrate for imposing unpopular taxes and other measures on them without any regard for their grievances.

Many Americans face "hunger crisis" as food insecurity rises
BY AIMEE PICCHI
MAY 31, 2023 / 8:14 AM / MONEYWATCH

Anti-hunger advocates say the U.S. is facing an "unprecedented" rise in food insecurity amid persistently high inflation in the grocery aisle and cuts to the food-stamp program earlier this year.

The rise in food insecurity — lacking enough food to live a healthy, active life — comes as the nation has ended the pandemic emergency and the economy, by many measures, continues to be strong. The unemployment rate is near a 50-year low, while wages have been rising for many workers. 

But those figures hide a stark reality that's affecting a growing share of U.S. households, ranging from young families to older Americans. Although jobs are plentiful, many employees don't earn enough to cover the surging cost of living, pushing some to make tradeoffs like skipping meals. 

And cuts to the food-stamp program earlier this year reduced benefits at a time when groceries are 20% costlier than two years ago. That caused food insecurity to jump to "unprecedented levels" in May among food-stamp recipients, according to a new survey from Propel, which makes an app for beneficiaries to check balances for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, (formerly known as food stamps).

About 44% of respondents reported skipping meals in the last month, a 7% increase and a record high, Propel noted. Those findings were echoed in a new study from the Greater Boston Food Bank, which found that some local families are making desperate choices, such as watering down baby formula or other food. 

"When I see one in three households with children reporting that their children were hungry, or they skipped a meal, that shouldn't happen," said Catherine D'Amato, CEO of the Greater Boston Food Bank, told CBS MoneyWatch. "This shows this is a hunger crisis that is persisting in Massachusetts."

D'Amato said that current rates of food insecurity are the highest she has ever seen in her career. Her group's study, released Tuesday, found that 33% of Massachusetts households were food insecure in 2022, while 36% of those with children didn't have enough food last year. 

The research jibes with findings from the U.S. Census, which for three years has asked households about their food consumption. The number of Americans who say they sometimes don't have enough to eat has jumped 23% — from 15.8 million prior to the pandemic to 19.2 million in the most recent survey, taken in late April and early May. 

New food-stamp work requirements
The rise in food insecurity comes as the debt ceiling deal, struck between the White House and Republican lawmakers, would add more work requirements to SNAP. That could create more hardship for a greater number of struggling Americans, D'Amato predicted. 

"The SNAP cuts and the work requirements are really going to be harmful," she added. "We don't know to what extent until we see the final debt ceiling agreements and how it gets rolled out."

SNAP already includes work requirements for low-income people ages 18 to 49 who are able-bodied and without dependents. Under the deal, that age limit would be raised to 54 years old, which could hurt older workers without a stable income and potentially put them at risk of losing food aid, experts said. 

However, the deal would temporarily eliminate SNAP work requirements for veterans and those experiencing homelessness, regardless of age. Those exceptions, as well as the higher age limit for work requirements, would expire in 2030.

About 700,000 people between the ages of 50 to 54 would be impacted by the new work requirements, according to the Wall Street Journal. But by eliminating work requirements for veterans and homeless people, about 78,000 people would gain benefits each month, the Congressional Budget Office said in a Tuesday report. 

Together, the changes to SNAP would boost government spending by $2.1 billion over the next decade, the CBO estimated.

Tradeoffs: Groceries or rent?
In the meantime, low-income Americans are increasingly making tradeoffs and experiencing broader hardships as they cope with the rising cost of groceries and cuts to their food aid, research shows. Eviction rates for food-stamp recipients soared by 40% from April to May, while 11% of respondents had their utilities cut off in the last month, a 24% jump from the prior month, Propel found.

A majority of households in Massachusetts who experienced food insecurity last year reporting having to decide between paying for food or covering rent, utilities and other costs, the Greater Boston Food Bank found. And almost one-third said they had watered down food or infant formula to make ends meet, while 85% said they bought the cheapest food available. 

"You hear this in health care, that 'I skipped my medication for a day'," but now people are making these same choices with food, D'Amato said. "It's shocking, though not surprising, that families are in a situation where they have to make tradeoffs."

During the Edo period (1603-1868), the obi evolved into a decorative accessory, as fashion trends shifted towards more elaborate and ornate clothing styles. Wealthy women in particular began wearing extravagant obis made from luxurious materials like silk, brocade, and velvet. These obis were often adorned with intricate embroidery, bold patterns, and vibrant colors.

The popularity of the obi can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, it allowed women to display their wealth and social status through the quality and design of their obi. The wider and more elaborate the obi, the more prestigious the wearer. Secondly, the obi provided a way for women to express themselves creatively through fashion, as they could choose from a wide variety of designs and colors to complement their kimono. Finally, the obi helped to cinch in the waistline, creating a flattering silhouette and emphasizing the female form.

Today, the obi remains an essential part of traditional Japanese dress, and continues to evolve and adapt with changing fashion trends. Modern obis may feature contemporary designs and materials, while still preserving the classic elegance and functionality of this iconic piece of Japanese culture.

Background:

The history of rock music has been volatile and unpredictable as the genre has constantly redefined and reinvented itself since its emergence in the late 1940s. Not surprisingly, then, it can be difficult to apply a straightforward definition to such a restless musical format.

But while people might quibble over specifics, rock music can generally be described as hard-edged music performed with electric guitars, bass, and drums and usually accompanied by lyrics sung by a vocalist. That sounds simple enough, but a closer look at the evolution of rock suggests how different styles and influences have shaped its development over the years.

Rock’s origins can be traced to the late 1940s, when the popular styles of the day, country music and blues, morphed into a new sound aided by electric guitars and a steady drumbeat. Pioneering rock artists of the 1950s such as Chuck Berry leaned heavily on classic blues structures while demonstrating a flair as natural-born entertainers. In contrast to the safe pop music of the era, rock’s aggressive attack suggested a sexual freedom that was shocking during that conservative age.

By the early '60s, Berry’s followers, most notably the Rolling Stones, expanded rock’s scope by transitioning from singles artists into musicians capable of producing cohesive albums of songs. Embracing sex and youthful rebellion in their music, the Stones courted controversy but also elevated rock to new cultural heights.

As rock music became the dominant form of popular music, new bands built on their predecessors’ strengths while branching out into new sonic territory. Led Zeppelin gave rock a darker, heavier tone, becoming one of the '70s’ most popular bands and helping to kick-start a new genre known as hard rock or heavy metal.

Around the same time, Pink Floyd added psychedelic elements and complex arrangements, creating concept albums tied together by a single theme and meant to be absorbed in a single sitting. Albums such as "Dark Side of the Moon" were credited with spawning the progressive rock movement.

In the late '70s, in response to what they perceived as pretentious “hippie” bands such as Pink Floyd, groups including the Sex Pistols and the Clash simplified rock to its core ingredients: loud guitars, rude attitude, and enraged singing. Punk was born.

While all three movements enjoyed different degrees of mainstream acceptance, a fourth, less-recognized style was beginning to take shape. Spotlighting atonal noise and unconventional rock instruments such as drum machines, groups such as Pere Ubu became the pioneers of industrial rock, an abrasive sub-genre that didn’t enjoy widespread popularity but inspired future rock bands.

As the '80s began, mainstream rock was losing commercial steam, its sound growing stale. In such a creatively stagnant environment, subgenres started to assert their dominance.

Inspired by punk’s outsider status and industrial’s eclectic instrumentation, keyboard-driven English bands such as Depeche Mode demonstrated a more introverted songwriting style, creating post-punk, also described as new wave.

Meanwhile, American groups including R.E.M. toyed with post-punk elements, balancing introspective lyrics with traditional rock-band arrangements. These bands were dubbed college rock because of their popularity on college radio stations.

By the end of the '80s, college rock had become such a lucrative alternative to mainstream rock that it received a new moniker: alternative rock. It was also called indie rock because the bands were often signed to small, independently owned labels.

Alternative rock cemented its cultural standing when the music magazine Billboard created a new chart in 1988 for alternative rock, which the publication classified as modern rock. For most music fans, terms such as modern rock, alternative, and indie are synonymous ways of describing this popular sub-genre.

prompt: What are some examples of might in the English language? Why is might used instead of can in some sentences?
response_a:
Might is a modal auxiliary verb in English that expresses possibility, probability, or potentiality in a less definite or strong way than can or will. Here are some examples:

1. Might be: This construction is used to express a lower degree of certainty or probability than the simple present form "is" or "are". For example, "The weather might be sunny tomorrow" suggests that there is a possibility, but it's not necessarily going to happen.

2. Might have been: This construction is used to express hypothetical situations in the past. For instance, "She might have passed the exam if she had studied harder" implies that it's possible that she could have succeeded.

3. Might as well: This idiomatic expression means "there is no reason not to" or "might just as well". For example, "I might as well go home now since my friends left already."

Might is often used instead of can for various reasons:

- To indicate a lesser degree of certainty or probability: When we use might instead of can, it usually suggests that something is possible, but less likely to occur. For instance, "He might win the lottery" has a lower degree of certainty compared to "He can win the lottery".

- To convey politeness: In some cases, using might instead of can is more polite or diplomatic, especially when making requests or suggestions. For example, "You might consider changing your mind" sounds more tentative and less forceful than "You can change your mind".

- To avoid overconfidence: Sometimes, using might helps to avoid overstating our opinions or predictions, which can make us sound more confident than we actually are. By using might, we can express our views more cautiously and humbly. For instance, "The market might continue to grow" seems less assertive than "The market can continue to grow".

In summary, might is a versatile word that can add nuance and complexity to our speech, helping us to communicate with greater precision and sensitivity.

3. Mars Global Surveyor (1996): This orbiter circled Mars for over two years, collecting detailed maps and images of the planet's surface. It also helped scientists better understand Mars' atmosphere and climate.

4. Mars Odyssey (2001): This mission sent an orbiter around Mars to study the planet's geology, atmosphere, and potential for past or present microbial life. It also discovered evidence of water ice at the planet's poles.

5. Mars Exploration Rover missions (Spirit and Opportunity, launched in 2003): These rovers were designed to search for evidence of past water activity on Mars. Both rovers exceeded their planned mission durations and provided valuable insights into the geology and history of Mars.

6. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (2005): This mission is currently in operation and has provided high-resolution images and topographic maps of Mars' surface. It has also assisted in locating possible landing sites for future missions.

7. MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN) (2013): This mission is studying the upper atmosphere of Mars to better understand how it has evolved over time and why Mars lost most of its atmosphere.

8. InSight (Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport) (2018): This mission involves placing a seismometer and heat probe on the surface of Mars to better understand the planet's interior structure and dynamics.

In marketing, a push strategy involves pushing or actively promoting products from the supplier to the intermediaries (distributors, wholesalers, or retailers) with the hope that they will further distribute it to the end consumers. This strategy is often used when there is a large number of intermediaries involved in the distribution process. The manufacturer takes the lead in initiating and managing the promotion, advertising, and sales activities. Examples of push strategies include trade shows, sales promotions, and direct mail campaigns.

On the other hand, a pull strategy is a marketing approach where the focus is on creating demand for the product directly among the end consumers. The manufacturer relies less on intermediaries and more on consumer-driven demand. The company uses various tools like advertising, branding, and packaging to attract and engage customers. Pull strategies aim to increase awareness, build loyalty, and stimulate repeat purchases by meeting the needs and preferences of the target audience. Some examples of pull strategies include celebrity endorsements, social media campaigns, and content marketing.

In summary, while push strategies rely on suppliers pushing products through intermediaries to reach the final consumer, pull strategies concentrate on drawing customers to purchase the product directly from the manufacturer. Both approaches have their advantages and disadvantages depending on the nature of the industry, product, and target market.
response_b:
In marketing, a push strategy involves pushing a product from the manufacturer to the distributor and then to the retailer for sale to the end consumer. This strategy relies on the company's sales force and distribution channels to move the product through the supply chain. The focus is on promoting the product to intermediaries, such as wholesalers and retailers, rather than directly to consumers. Examples of push strategies include trade shows, sales promotions, and advertising targeted at intermediaries.

On the other hand, a pull strategy focuses on drawing the product directly to the consumer through demand generation. This strategy aims to create customer awareness and desire for the product, which will lead to increased demand and eventually, sales. Pull strategies rely on effective communication and promotion to target audiences, such as social media campaigns, content marketing, and influencer partnerships. Unlike a push strategy, the focus is not solely on selling to intermediaries but also on building relationships with consumers.

In summary, while a push strategy pushes products through the supply chain, a pull strategy pulls products directly to the consumer through demand generation. Both strategies have their advantages and disadvantages, and the choice between them depends on various factors such as the type of product, target audience, and market conditions.

What is Color Gamut?
Color gamut is defined as the range of colors which a particular device can produce or record. It is usually shown by an enclosed area of the primary colors of the device on the chromaticity diagram. For example, the primary colors of monitors are red, green, and blue. Hence, the color gamut of a monitor is shown in a triangular area enclosed by the color coordinates of the monitor's red, green, and blue colors. A chromaticity diagram with different color gamuts is shown in Figure 1.

Color Gamut in CIE 1931 xy Color Coordinates
One very important aspect of color gamuts is that they're three dimensional, not two dimensional. When we describe a color, it usually consists of three components: hue, saturation, and brightness. Since color gamut is a collection of colors, it is logical that it can also be described using hue, saturation, and brightness. So when we plot a color gamut, it should be a three dimensional graph as shown in Figure 2. However, plotting a three dimensional graph is never an easy job, even nowadays. As a result, we often use a two dimensional graph to represent a color gamut, as shown in Figure 1. The missing dimension is brightness, which is perpendicular to the screen or sheet of paper.

Commonly Seen Color Gamut Standards
The most commonly known color gamut might be “NTSC” (established in 1953 by the US FCC), however, it is not a standard color gamut. “sRGB” is the standard color gamut established by the IEC in 1999. The reason for standardizing a color gamut was to promote an easier way for color reproduction. If all color-utilizing devices, including digital cameras, scanners, monitors, printers, and projectors, can reproduce the sRGB color gamut correctly, then images can be reproduced very consistently across devices. This phenomenon is due to devices having the same capability of recording (with proper calibration of course), displaying, or printing the same range of colors, so for the same image, the variation of color reproduced on different devices will be limited. Hence, color fidelity or color management could be achieved. This is also known as the concept of reproducing in-gamut colors.
However, in order to achieve color fidelity or color management, the exact RGB color coordinates on the chromaticity diagram must be agreed upon. Each pair of color coordinates specifies a distinct or unique color. For example, (x, y) = (0.64, 0.30) is not equal to (x, y) = (0.63, 0.29), even though the numbers are very close to each other. In the display industry, there is also another piece of misleading information. Some panel manufactures or display brands market their monitors as “72% NTSC” in terms of color gamut, claiming to be “sRGB compatible”. Unfortunately, this is not the case. If we take the color coordinates from each color gamut from Table 1 and calculate the area of each color gamut, we can find that the area ratio of sRGB to NTSC is 0.72 to 1. This is where the misleading concept of 72% NTSC equals to sRGB came from. The correct interpretation is “the number of colors that sRGB can reproduce is the same as 72% of NTSC, but the colors being reproduced are not necessarily the same colors.” Because the only constraint on 72% is the area ratio, and there is no information about the RGB color coordinates. Hence, we cannot say 72% NTSC color gamut is equal to sRGB color gamut. Therefore, it only makes sense when we talk about “coverage rate” when comparing two color gamuts. An example can be seen in Figure 3. On the left-hand side, both color gamuts have the same area ratio, but they do not 100% cover each other. On the right-hand side, only a certain amount of the monitor color gamut covers sRGB, and it's not 100%. It is clear that this particular monitor cannot reproduce 100% of the sRGB color gamut.

Of course, there are a lot more color gamuts other than NTSC and sRGB out there. For example, AdobeRGB, DCI-P3, EBU, and AppleRGB. They all have their own RGB color coordinates and associated white points and brightness specifications, and of course their own application. For example, AdobeRGB is meant for use in graphic design, mainly for printing purposes. DCI-P3 is mainly used in digital cinema, and EBU is used by the European broadcasting industry. Rec. 2020 is a newly developed standard for all devices in the future, and it represents almost all the colors humans can perceive.

Which Color Gamut Should I Choose?
The selection of color gamut really depends on your workflow and requirements. If you are working mainly with photos and your final output will be hardcopy prints, then AdobeRGB may be your best choice of color gamut in your workflow. If your output is online albums or shared on Facebook, then it is suggested you edit your photos in the AdobeRGB color gamut to keep the most colors, then convert to sRGB before posting online. Because currently internet browsers only support sRGB as a color gamut, any color gamut larger than sRGB is considered a “wide color gamut”, and will not be handled correctly. So if your photos are manipulated or enhanced in the AdobeRGB color gamut, when posted online, the photo may look quite pale and desaturated. Therefore, the best practice to avoid this disaster is to convert the photos to sRGB before posting online.

If you are working with videos, the latest trend is to move from Rec. 709 to DCI-P3 or Display P3. DCI stands for Digital Cinema Initiative, and P3 refers to a set of viewing conditions. Modern movie theaters can fully reproduce the vivid color gamut used by digital cinema projection systems. However, the white point of DCI-P3 was chosen to be a greenish white due to projection system configurations. Apple, YouTube, Netflix and other video content providers have adopted the same color gamut as DCI-P3 but utilized D65 as a white point and renamed the gamut Display P3. A neutral white is more welcome in most monitors and TVs, and gaining popularity among video post-production professionals.

Summary
In this article, we learned the definition of color gamut and what is the representation on a chromaticity diagram. Color gamut should be represented in three dimensional graphs but reduced to two dimensional graphs for easier representation. We also talked about the reason for standardizing a color gamut, sRGB, to facilitate in-gamut color matching across different devices. Furthermore, the misleading concept of 72% NTSC being equal to sRGB was also discussed and clarified. Equal color gamut areas do not necessarily guarantee the same color rendering capability. Instead, coverage rate should be looked at when comparing two color gamuts. At last, we looked at different color gamuts and their applications. We also learned how to choose the correct color gamut and maintain color consistency for posting photos online.

A golden harvest is reaped by hand,
Dried blades of green now take on hues of beige,
This humble grain, called hay, we'll understand.

The fragrance lingers sweetly in the air,
A scent of summertime that never fades,
As barns and stables fill with this amber share,
And livestock graze upon its nourished shades.

Here lies a source of life, a simple gift,
Of nature's bounty, freely given still,
It offers strength and sustenance to uplift,
And helps us face each day with willful skill.

With rustling whispers, hay invites our soul,
To find a peace that comes from simple things,
And so we pause, and let our spirits roll,
In harmony with nature's gentle strings.

Oh, hay, your beauty speaks of life renewed,
A symbol of our earth, a humble good.
response_b:

A harvest grows that time will stay,
The golden grain, so rich and rare,
Is but a prelude to this humble fare.

For in these hills, where cows do graze,
A bale of hay, a treasure is displayed,
Its brown and green hues, like autumn's shade,
Are woven tight by winds, that gently swayed.

The fragrance of this earthy scene,
Is sweet and heady, like a dream serene,
Of clover, grass, and sun-kissed dew,
It fills the nose with scents anew.

Within this bundle, soft and dense,
The animals find sustenance, as they sense
The taste of earth, the gentle rain,
That feeds their souls, and eases pain.

Oh hay, thy humble worth we see,
Thou dost not wane, nor e'er decay,
But evermore, art here to stay,
And nourish life, on land or bay.

This gift of nature, with a grateful face,
For hay, is more than just a feed,
It's life itself, for all who need.

prompt: What is the human mind and how does it work? How do our thoughts, emotions, and behaviors affect our well-being, and what practices and interventions can promote mental health and wellness?
response_a:
The human mind is a complex and dynamic system that encompasses various cognitive processes, emotions, and behaviors. It involves the interaction of different brain structures and neural networks, which allow us to perceive, reason, remember, and make decisions. However, the precise mechanisms by which the mind works are still not fully understood, and there is ongoing research in this area.

One model that has gained popularity in recent years is the tripartite model of the mind, which proposes that the mind consists of three main components: the conscious mind, the subconscious mind, and the unconscious mind. The conscious mind is responsible for our immediate perceptions and experiences, while the subconscious mind stores our memories, beliefs, and habits. The unconscious mind contains our innate drives, instincts, and impulses.

Our thoughts, emotions, and behaviors have a significant impact on our well-being, both positive and negative. Positive thinking, gratitude, and optimism have been linked to better physical and mental health outcomes, while negative thoughts, rumination, and pessimism can lead to depression, anxiety, and stress. Emotions also play a crucial role in shaping our behavior and decision-making processes, and learning to regulate them effectively can improve our overall well-being.

Practices and interventions that promote mental health and wellness include mindfulness meditation, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), exercise, social support, and self-care. Mindfulness meditation involves focusing one's attention on the present moment, which can help reduce stress and improve emotional regulation. CBT is a type of talk therapy that helps individuals identify and challenge negative thought patterns and replace them with more positive ones. prompt: What is a passive house and how does it differ from an energy-efficient house?
response_a:
A passive house (also known as Passivhaus) is a type of building that is designed to be extremely energy-efficient and minimizes the need for active heating and cooling systems. It achieves this by implementing several key features, such as:

1. Airtight construction: Passive houses are built with very little air leakage, which helps to prevent drafts and keeps the indoor environment comfortable without relying on mechanical ventilation.

2. High levels of insulation: The walls, roof, and floors of passive houses are heavily insulated to reduce heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer.

3. Triple-pane windows: Passive houses use high-performance windows with multiple panes of glass and low-emissivity coatings to minimize heat transfer through the glass.

4. Passive solar design: Passive houses are oriented to take advantage of the sun's natural warmth during winter months, while shading devices are used to block direct sunlight during summer months.

Compared to an energy-efficient house, a passive house goes beyond just reducing energy consumption. While energy-efficient houses aim to lower energy bills, passive houses strive for net-zero energy consumption, meaning they produce as much energy as they consume. Passive houses achieve this through the implementation of renewable energy sources like solar panels or wind turbines, in addition to the previously mentioned features. In summary, a passive house is a more rigorous and comprehensive approach to energy efficiency than an energy-efficient house.
response_b:
A Passive House, also known as a Passivhaus, is a rigorous standard for energy-efficient building design that aims to minimize a building's ecological footprint by reducing its energy consumption and carbon emissions. It is different from an energy-efficient house in several ways:

1. Passive House standards are more stringent than those for energy-efficient houses. While both types of buildings aim to conserve energy, Passive Houses have much tighter requirements for insulation, air tightness, ventilation, and heat recovery.

2. Passive House designs prioritize passive solar design principles, such as orientation and shading, over active systems like HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) units. This means that Passive Houses rely more on natural light, heat, and ventilation to regulate indoor temperatures and humidity levels.

3. Passive House buildings are certified by an independent third party organization, which ensures that they meet the strictest standards for energy efficiency, comfort, and durability. Energy-efficient houses may not undergo this certification process.

4. Passive House buildings are designed to significantly reduce heating and cooling costs, resulting in lower operating expenses and higher savings compared to traditional or energy-efficient houses.

In summary, while both Passive Houses and energy-efficient houses aim to conserve energy, Passive Houses take a more holistic approach to energy efficiency, prioritizing passive design strategies and rigorous certification standards to achieve superior performance in terms of comfort, health, and sustainability.

prompt: What is the history of the slipper and how did it come to be?
response_a:
The history of the slipper can be traced back to ancient times, where they were worn primarily for practical purposes such as protection and warmth. In ancient Egypt, both men and women wore simple, flat-soled shoes made from materials like leather or papyrus. These shoes had no distinctive features that would later define modern slippers.

In the Middle Ages, Europeans began wearing shoes with pointed toes and high heels, which were impractical for indoor wear. Indoor shoes, also known as "slippers," were introduced during this time as a more comfortable alternative. They were typically made from soft materials like velvet, silk, or fur and had low heels or no heel at all.

The design of slippers evolved over time, with different styles emerging in different parts of the world. In Asia, traditional slippers known as zori or tabi were worn by men and women as part of their everyday attire. These slippers featured a thong between the big toe and other toes, allowing them to fit snugly around the foot.

In the West, slippers became a symbol of luxury and comfort during the 18th century. Wealthy individuals began wearing decorative slippers made from fine materials like satin, silk, and velvet. These slippers often featured intricate embroidery, lace, or beading, making them works of art in their own right.

Today, slippers continue to evolve, with new materials and designs being introduced. Slippers have become a popular choice for both men and women due to their comfort and versatility. They are available in a wide range of styles, from classic loafers to trendy slip-on sneakers. Additionally, advancements in technology have led to the creation of slippers with added features such as heating and massage functions.

Overall, the slipper has come a long way since its humble beginnings as a practical indoor shoe. It has transformed into a fashionable and functional item that reflects the changing needs and preferences of society. Whether you prefer traditional or contemporary styles, there's a slipper out there that's perfect for you.
response_b:
The origin of the modern-day slipper can be traced back to the 1600s in Europe, where it was known as a "chamber shoe" or "house slipper." These early versions were typically made from soft leather and featured a low heel and closed toe, designed to provide comfort and warmth indoors.

Over time, the design of the slipper evolved to include more decorative elements, such as embroidery, tassels, and fur trim. In the 18th century, slippers became a popular accessory for both men and women, worn not only as indoor footwear but also as outdoor shoes in warmer months.

By the 19th century, slippers had become a fashionable item, particularly among the upper classes. They were often made from luxurious materials like silk, velvet, and satin, and featured intricate designs and embellishments. Men's slippers, in particular, came in a variety of styles, including Oxford, Balmoral, and Chelsea boots, all of which could be converted into slippers by removing the heels.

Today, slippers continue to evolve, with new materials and technologies being introduced to improve comfort and style. From fleece-lined slippers for winter to breathable mesh options for summer, there is a wide range of styles available to suit every preference and need.

In terms of cultural significance, slippers have played a role in various traditions and customs around the world. For example, in Japan, traditional slippers called zori are worn as part of tea ceremonies and other formal events, while in India, jutti slippers are commonly worn by both men and women as a symbol of cultural heritage.

In short, the history of the slipper is a long and fascinating one, reflecting both practical and aesthetic considerations over time. Whether worn for comfort, style, or tradition, slippers continue to be a beloved and versatile part of many people's wardrobes today.

Lucy Lippard—a giant of American art criticism, author of more than 20 books, and co-founder of Printed Matter, the quintessential seller of books made by artists—turned 80 this year. Despite her multitude of other accomplishments, Lippard is best known for “The Dematerialization of Art,” an essay she co-authored in 1968 with John Chandler (available online here.) In the essay, Lippard presented evidence that art might be entering a phase of pure intellectualism, the result of which could be the complete disappearance of the traditional art object. The piece grew out of, and helped contextualize, the preceding decade or so of wildly inventive conceptual art, which often left behind only ephemeral, non-archival relics, or no relics at all other than perhaps recordings of experiences. Conceptual artists were devoted to making ideas the central focus of their work, and many argued convincingly that the objects artists make to express their ideas are nothing but waste products, and that the ideas themselves are the only things worthy of consideration. The essay was enormously influential at the time: so much so that Lippard followed it up with a book called Six Years, extensively analyzing evidence of the trend. But obviously in the long run her premonition was inaccurate since art objects still have yet to dematerialize. Nonetheless, in celebration of the upcoming 50th anniversary of the original publication of The Dematerialization of Art, we thought we would take a moment to delve into this influential essay and highlight what about it is relevant for our time.

Lippard based the core concepts she discussed in The Dematerialization of Art on an idea first laid out in a book called The Mathematical Basis of the Arts, written by the American painter Joseph Schillinger. In that book, Schillinger divided all of art history into five categories of aesthetic phenomena. First, he explained, came the “pre-aesthetic” phase of mimicry. Next came ritualistic or religious art. Then came emotional art. Then rational, empirical-based art. And then the fifth, and allegedly “final” aesthetic phase described by Schillinger was “scientific,” or what he called “post-aesthetic.” This final phase, he predicted, would culminate in the “liberation of the idea” and lead to the “disintegration of art.”

While contemplating the evolution of art throughout the 1950s and 60s, Lippard believed what she was witnessing was the emergence of this fifth phase of art. And she was excited about the notion. She considered dematerialization a positive, vital shift. After all, if the aesthetic object could cease to exist as the central focus of art then art could be freed from commodification, the often vile system that exerts so much destructive force on the lives and work of many artists.

As evidence that dematerialization had begun, Lippard cited movements such as Light and Space, which were visual but not object-based, and Minimalism, which drastically pared down the aesthetic object. Such movements she believed diminished the importance of the visual aspect of an artwork, defining the visual as more of a jumping-off point for an immaterial, intellectual experience. But one of the early, and obvious, criticisms of The Dematerialization of Art was that even though these ephemeral, conceptual concepts were less object-based, they still nonetheless resulted in physical phenomena. Even a performance artist creates a thing—a performance—which can be sold as an experience, or recorded.

No matter how slight a relic an artist creates, it can become fetishized and traded as a commodity. The only way to completely avoid the possibility of commodification is to never share an idea: then perhaps the reverence and sanctity of the intellectual experience can be preserved. But only shared ideas can truly be called art. And as soon as an idea is shared, it can be possessed, manipulated, and expressed in other ways, or other words, materialized. And as soon as something materializes it can be bought and sold as a commodity.

 Re-reading The Dematerialization of Art today, the only true error that seems evident is how it presents the five phases of art, as explained by Schillinger, as something linear. It is always tempting for each generation to see itself as standing at the forefront of modernity. Schillinger thought art had been progressing historically through phases, and Lippard thought she was part of the generation that was advancing art toward its evolutionary apex. But time does not move forward; it just passes. Culture is not linear; it repeats itself. Humanity devolves as rapidly as it evolves. And the truth was in the 1960s and 70s, and still is today, that artists are finding ways to dematerialize as rapidly as others are rediscovering how to materialize it.

Ultimately, Lippard must have also realized this even as she wrote on the topic of dematerialization because her essay concludes by asking if the so-called zero point in art is likely to be reached soon. The answer, she states, is, “It hardly seems likely.” Even today as artists sell virtual creations that exist only in digital space, we can still argue dematerialization is a fantasy. Anything that can be seen is by definition material, even if it can only be seen through virtual reality goggles. But in our opinion that only proves that perhaps achieving dematerialization was never really the point. The point Lippard was truly making was simply that one important aspect of visual art is to engage tirelessly in the search to discover how to express more with less. Any artist working toward dematerialization is also working toward simplicity. And simplicity leads to the discovery of what is truly indispensable, and thus truly meaningful. That is not the final phase of art. But it is capable of reminding us what the value of art truly is.
